questions.question: What is object-oriented programming and why was it created? How does it differ from procedural programming?
questions.title: What Is OOP and Why It Exists — Procedural vs Object-Oriented
questions.direct_answer: Object-oriented programming is a paradigm that organizes software around objects — bundles of state (fields) and behavior (methods) that model real-world entities — rather than around functions and procedures acting on shared global data. It was created to solve the problems procedural programming hit at scale: tangled global state, functions that knew too much about each other's data, and code that was impossible to change without breaking something far away. OOP's four pillars (encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction) each attack a specific failure mode of procedural code. Java is a class-based, statically-typed OOP language where every program lives inside a class.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand OOP as a solution to a real problem (managing complexity at scale) rather than a set of syntax rules to memorize. Interviewers open with this to check if you can reason about paradigms, not just recite the four pillars.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Answering 'OOP is about classes and objects' without explaining WHY the paradigm shift happened — what problem procedural code had that objects solve. Equally bad: listing the four pillars without connecting each to the failure mode it prevents.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the specific procedural failure modes (shared mutable state, scattered responsibility, rigid function dependencies) and map each pillar to the one it fixes. Mention that OOP is not the only paradigm (functional, declarative) and know when it's the wrong choice.

sections.title: OOP Is a Response to a Problem, Not a Set of Keywords
sections.content:
Before object-oriented programming, the dominant paradigm was procedural: you wrote functions, and those functions operated on data that lived in shared, global structures. A banking app was a set of functions (`deposit()`, `withdraw()`, `transfer()`) all reading and writing the same `accountBalance` variable. That works for 100 lines. At 100,000 lines it collapses — any function can corrupt any data, there's no way to know who owns what, and changing a data structure means hunting every function that touches it.

OOP was created in the late 1960s (Simula, then Smalltalk) to solve this. The idea: instead of scattering data across globals and letting any function mutate it, bundle the data and the operations on that data into a single unit — an object. The object owns its state and exposes only a controlled interface. You don't call `withdraw(account, 500)`; you call `account.withdraw(500)`, and the account object enforces its own rules.

Java is a class-based OOP language: you define a class (the blueprint) and instantiate objects (the runtime instances). Every method and field lives inside a class — there are no standalone functions. This is a design choice, not a limitation: it forces you to think about which object owns each piece of behavior.

sections.title: Procedural vs Object-Oriented — The Real Difference
sections.content:
| Dimension | Procedural | Object-Oriented |
|---|---|---|
| Organizing unit | Functions operating on data | Objects bundling state + behavior |
| Data ownership | Shared, global, anyone can mutate | Encapsulated inside the object that owns it |
| Change impact | Changing a data struct breaks every function using it | Changing internal state only affects the object's own methods |
| Mental model | "What steps do I execute?" | "Which objects interact, and what messages do they send?" |
| Reuse | Copy-paste functions, shared libraries | Inheritance, composition, polymorphism |
| Failure mode | Spaghetti — everything depends on everything | Over-engineering — too many layers, unnecessary abstractions |
| Languages | C, Pascal, early Fortran | Java, Python, C#, Kotlin, Ruby |

sections.title: The Problem OOP Solves: Shared Mutable State
sections.content:
Here's the procedural version of a bank account. The balance is a global variable. Any function can set it to anything.

The problem: `processFees()` can set balance to -1000 without the account knowing. `transfer()` can read a half-updated balance. There's no owner of the data — it's a free-for-all. At scale, this is how you get bugs that nobody can reproduce because the state depends on the order of every function call in the system.

sections.title: Procedural — Any Function Can Corrupt Any Data
OOP — The Object Owns Its State and Enforces Its Rules
How Each Pillar Maps to a Procedural Failure Mode
sections.content:
The four pillars aren't arbitrary — each one fixes a specific thing that went wrong in procedural code.

**Encapsulation** fixes *shared mutable state*. Data is private; only the owning object's methods can mutate it. You can't have `processFees()` silently writing to `accountBalance` because balance is `private`.

**Abstraction** fixes *depending on implementation details*. In procedural code, you call `sortArray(arr)` and you know it's a bubble sort because you can see it. In OOP, you depend on a `Sortable` interface — you don't know or care how it sorts. When the implementation changes from bubble to quicksort, no caller breaks.

**Inheritance** fixes *duplicated code across similar types*. Without it, `Dog` and `Cat` each copy-paste the `breathe()`, `eat()`, `sleep()` methods. With it, both extend `Animal` and inherit the shared behavior. (In modern Java, prefer composition over inheritance — but the code-reuse mechanism exists for a reason.)

**Polymorphism** fixes *type-switching code*. Procedural code does `if (type == DOG) bark(); else if (type == CAT) meow();` and you edit that function every time you add an animal. OOP does `animal.makeSound()` and each object responds in its own way — adding a new type means writing a new class, not editing existing code.

sections.title: When OOP Is the Wrong Tool
sections.content:
OOP is not universally superior. It excels when you have entities with state and behavior that interact (domain models, UI components, game entities). It's the wrong choice when:

- **The problem is data transformation, not entity interaction.** A pipeline that reads CSV → filters rows → writes JSON is functional programming territory, not OOP. Forcing it into `CSVReader` + `RowFilter` + `JSONWriter` objects adds ceremony without value. Java's Stream API is an admission of this — it's functional, not object-oriented.
- **Statelessness is the goal.** HTTP request handlers, pure computations, event-sourced systems — these work better functionally. A `Calculator` object with no state is just a namespace for functions.
- **Performance-critical tight loops.** Object allocation, virtual method dispatch, and indirection have costs. Game engines, numerical kernels, and embedded systems often drop to procedural or data-oriented design for the hot path.

The mark of a senior developer is knowing when OOP helps and when it's ceremony. Java pushes you toward OOP by design (everything is a class), but the best Java code uses functional patterns (streams, lambdas, records) where objects would just be overhead.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **OOP organizes software around objects** (state + behavior bundled together) instead of functions operating on shared data.
- **It was created to manage complexity** — procedural code collapses at scale because any function can corrupt any data.
- **Each pillar fixes a specific procedural failure**: encapsulation (shared state), abstraction (implementation dependence), inheritance (code duplication), polymorphism (type-switching code).
- **Java is class-based OOP** — every method and field lives in a class; there are no standalone functions.
- **OOP is not always the right paradigm** — data-transform pipelines and stateless logic are better served functionally.
- **The interviewer wants to hear WHY, not just WHAT** — explain the problem the paradigm solves, then the pillars as solutions.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Object-oriented programming is a paradigm that organizes code around objects — bundles of state and behavior — instead of functions operating on shared data. It was created to solve a real problem: procedural code collapses at scale because any function can corrupt any global variable, and changing a data structure means finding every function that touches it.

In OOP, the object owns its state and exposes a controlled interface. You don't call withdraw(account, 500) — you call account.withdraw(500), and the account enforces its own rules like "balance can't go negative." That's encapsulation: the first pillar.

The four pillars each fix a specific procedural failure mode. Encapsulation fixes shared mutable state — data is private, only the owning object can mutate it. Abstraction fixes depending on implementation details — you program to an interface, not a concrete class, so swapping the implementation doesn't break callers. Inheritance fixes duplicated code across similar types. Polymorphism fixes type-switching code — instead of if-dog-else-if-cat, each object responds to the same message in its own way.

Java is class-based OOP — everything lives in a class. But I'd add that OOP isn't always the right tool. A CSV-to-JSON pipeline is a data transformation, and forcing it into objects adds ceremony. Java's Stream API is an acknowledgment that functional patterns belong in the language too. The senior distinction is knowing when OOP helps and when it's just ceremony.

questions.question: The Four Pillars of OOP — Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, Abstraction
questions.title: The Four Pillars of OOP — Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, Abstraction
questions.direct_answer: **Encapsulation** — private fields + behavior methods (`withdraw()` not `setBalance()`). **Inheritance** — IS-A via `extends`; no multiple via classes (diamond problem); IS-A test first. **Polymorphism** — overloading = compile-time (compiler picks), overriding = runtime (JVM picks by actual object type). **Abstraction** — interface = 100%, abstract class = partial; it's a design principle, not the `abstract` keyword. sections.title: The Four Pillars of OOP in Java — Quick Overview
sections.content:
Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) organizes code around **objects** — self-contained units that combine data (fields) and behavior (methods). A **class** is the blueprint; an **object** is an instance of that class. Create a `Dog` class with `name` and `breed` as fields and `bark()` and `eat()` as methods — every dog object you create from it gets the same structure.

Java's OOP is built on four core principles: **Encapsulation**, **Inheritance**, **Polymorphism**, and **Abstraction**. Each one solves a specific design problem — they're the rules for how objects protect their data, relate to each other, and hide complexity.

sections.title: Four Pillars at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Encapsulation|~Bundle data + methods in a class|private fields, public methods|expose behavior: withdraw()|class owns its invariants
blue|Inheritance|~Child acquires parent via extends|IS-A test before using it|no multiple via classes|prefer composition (HAS-A)
emerald|Polymorphism|~One entity, many forms|overloading = compile-time|overriding = runtime|JVM picks by actual object type
violet|Abstraction|~Hide how, show what|abstract class: 0-100%|interface: 100%|design principle, not a keyword

sections.title: Encapsulation: The Class Controls Its Own State
sections.content:
**Encapsulation** means bundling data (fields) and the methods that work on that data together inside a class, and restricting direct access from outside. The fields are the class's private state; the methods are the controlled access points.

Think of it like a medicine capsule — the active ingredients are sealed inside. You interact with the tablet as a whole, not with individual chemicals. A `BankAccount` works the same way: you don't reach in and modify `balance` directly; you call `withdraw()`.

- Declare fields `private`; expose only through public methods
- The key rule: expose **behavior**, not state — `account.withdraw(100)` is right; `account.setBalance(account.getBalance() - 100)` is not
- The class owns its logic — validation, overdraft checks, and audit logs live inside, invisible to callers
- If `balance` changes from `double` to `BigDecimal`, no caller breaks — they only ever called `withdraw()`

sections.title: Theater: private field, but the caller controls all logic
Real encapsulation: the class owns its invariants
Inheritance: Acquire Properties via IS-A
sections.content:
**Inheritance** lets a child class acquire the properties and methods of a parent class using the `extends` keyword. `Dog extends Animal` — the `Dog` class gets everything `Animal` has (`name`, `age`, `eat()`, `sleep()`) and can add its own (`bark()`) or override existing behavior.

This models an IS-A relationship. A dog **is** an animal. A cat **is** an animal. Unlike a car, which *has* an engine — that's not inheritance, that's composition. The IS-A test is how you decide which to use.

- **IS-A test first**: `Dog IS-A Animal` ✓ → `extends`. `Car HAS-A Engine` ✗ → use composition instead
- Java supports: single, multilevel (`Dog → Animal → Object`), hierarchical (`Dog, Cat → Animal`). Multiple inheritance via classes = **not allowed** (diamond problem)
- Prefer interfaces for multiple inheritance
- Deep hierarchies (4+ levels) = design smell; prefer flat hierarchies + composition

sections.title: Inheritance misused — hierarchy collapses
Composition — behaviors assembled, not inherited
Polymorphism: One Interface, Many Forms
sections.content:
**Polymorphism** means "many forms" — the same method name or interface behaves differently depending on the actual object type. A `Shape` can be a `Circle`, a `Rectangle`, or a `Triangle`. Call `shape.area()` on any of them — you get the right calculation without knowing which shape it is.

A useful real-world frame: a person behaves differently as a father at home, an employee at work, a student in class. Same person — many behaviors depending on context.

- **Compile-time (overloading)**: same method name, different parameters — compiler picks the right version at build time
- **Runtime (overriding)**: `Shape s = new Circle(); s.area()` — JVM picks `Circle`'s version based on the actual object type, not the reference type
- Without it: adding a new type means editing existing code — a growing `if-else` chain for every new variant
- With it: new type = new class, zero existing code touched

sections.title: Without polymorphism — adding ApplePay edits this method
With polymorphism — new type = new class, zero existing code touched
Abstraction: Depend on Contracts, Not Implementations
sections.content:
**Abstraction** means hiding the implementation details and showing only what the user needs. The "how" stays hidden; only the "what" is visible.

You use abstraction every day without thinking about it. A TV remote has a "volume up" button — you don't know the circuit board. An ATM lets you withdraw cash — the banking system behind it is invisible. That's abstraction: you see the interface, not the engine.

- `interface` = 100% abstraction — pure contract, no implementation detail exposed
- `abstract class` = partial abstraction — can have both abstract (no body) and concrete (with body) methods
- The practical daily rule: `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>()` — declare the interface type, not the concrete class. Swap to `LinkedList` — no caller changes
- The common confusion: `abstract` is a Java keyword; abstraction is a design *principle*. An `interface` achieves full abstraction without the `abstract` keyword at all

sections.title: Declare the interface type — never the concrete class
What Each Pillar Actually Protects You From
sections.content:
| Pillar | The Problem It Solves | Java Mechanism | What Breaks Without It |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Encapsulation** | External code depends on internal structure — any field change breaks callers | `private` fields, methods as the only access path | `int` → `long` field change cascades through every direct accessor |
| **Inheritance** | Shared behavior is copy-pasted — bug fixes need updating in N places | `extends`, `@Override`, `super` | Logging format change requires editing 15 classes instead of one parent |
| **Polymorphism** | Adding a new variant requires editing existing code | Method overriding, interfaces, overloading | New `PaymentMethod` forces editing `processPayment()` and retesting all paths |
| **Abstraction** | Callers coupled to implementation — swapping a library rewrites consumers | Interfaces, `abstract` classes | Replacing MySQL with PostgreSQL means rewriting every service that called it |

They reinforce each other: encapsulation makes polymorphism safe; abstraction guides where inheritance boundaries should be.

sections.title: Where All Four Pillars Converge in One Line
sections.content:
```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();  // all four pillars, one line
```

| Pillar | What it does here |
|---|---|
| **Abstraction** | `List` is the contract — implementation hidden from every caller |
| **Encapsulation** | `ArrayList`'s internal array is inaccessible to callers |
| **Polymorphism** | Any `List` implementation substitutes without changing callers |
| **Inheritance** | `ArrayList` fulfills the `List` contract via `implements` |

`ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>()` breaks all four — one word change couples every caller to that specific class.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Encapsulation** — `private` fields + behavior methods. Use `withdraw()`, not `setBalance()`.
- **Inheritance** — IS-A via `extends`. No multiple through classes (diamond problem). IS-A test first.
- **Polymorphism** — overloading = compile-time (compiler picks). Overriding = runtime (JVM picks by actual type).
- **Abstraction** — interface = 100%, abstract class = partial. Design *principle*, not the `abstract` keyword.
- **All four in one** — `List<String> list = new ArrayList<>()` uses every pillar simultaneously.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Object-Oriented Programming is just a way of organising code around objects — and an object is a self-contained unit that holds its own data along with the behaviour that works on that data. In Java, a class is the blueprint, and an object is what you get when you create — or instantiate — that class. So if I have a `Dog` class with `name` and `breed` as fields and `bark()` and `eat()` as methods, every dog object I create from it has the same shape but its own values.

The four pillars — Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, and Abstraction — are the design principles that govern how you build those objects so the system stays maintainable as it grows.

Encapsulation is about giving the class control over its own state. The fields stay `private`, and the only way to change them is through the methods the class exposes. So instead of letting the caller do `setBalance(getBalance() - 100)`, the `BankAccount` class offers `account.withdraw(100)` — and inside that method it validates the amount, checks for overdraft, logs the transaction, and updates the balance. The caller doesn't know how the balance is stored. If I change `balance` from `double` to `BigDecimal` later for precision, no caller breaks, because they never touched the field directly. That's what encapsulation buys you — it isolates change.

Inheritance is the IS-A relationship between classes, expressed through the `extends` keyword. `Dog extends Animal` means a `Dog` is an `Animal` — it inherits the parent's fields and methods, can override behaviour, and can add its own. Before reaching for it, I run the IS-A test: a dog is an animal, so inheritance fits; but a car has an engine, so that's composition, not inheritance. Java only allows single inheritance through classes — you can't `extends` two parents — and the reason is the diamond problem, where two parents could provide conflicting versions of the same method. For multiple inheritance, you use interfaces.

Polymorphism literally means 'many forms' — the same method call behaves differently depending on the actual object. There are two kinds. Compile-time polymorphism is method overloading: same method name, different parameters, and the compiler picks the right version at build time. Runtime polymorphism is method overriding — `Shape s = new Circle(); s.area()` runs `Circle.area()`, because the JVM looks at the actual object type at runtime, not at the type of the variable. Without polymorphism, adding a new payment method means editing every `if-else` chain; with it, you just add a new class.

Abstraction is hiding the implementation details and exposing only what the caller needs. An `interface` is full abstraction — pure contract, no implementation detail. An `abstract class` is partial — it can mix abstract methods with concrete ones. The everyday version of abstraction is writing `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>()` instead of `ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>()`. By depending on the `List` contract, you can swap to `LinkedList` tomorrow and zero callers change.

The four work as a system, not a checklist. Encapsulation is what makes polymorphism safe — because the class controls its own invariants, you can substitute one implementation for another without breaking callers. Abstraction is what tells you where inheritance boundaries should be. And that one line, `List<String> names = new ArrayList<>()`, actually uses all four at once: `List` is the abstraction, `ArrayList`'s internal array is encapsulated, any `List` implementation can substitute via polymorphism, and `ArrayList` satisfies the `List` contract through inheritance.

questions.question: Encapsulation and Access Modifiers in Java (private, protected, public, default)
questions.title: Encapsulation and Access Modifiers in Java (private, protected, public, default)
questions.direct_answer: **Encapsulation** = the class owns its own state via behavior methods (`withdraw()` not `setBalance()`). Java has **4 access levels**: `private` (this class only), default/package-private (no modifier — same package), `protected` (same package + subclasses elsewhere), `public` (everyone, permanently). Key trap: `protected` ≠ only subclasses — it includes the whole same package too.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands encapsulation beyond 'make fields private' — can they explain what each access modifier controls, when to use package-private vs protected, and what real encapsulation looks like in practice
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking encapsulation means private fields plus getters/setters. Not knowing that default (no modifier) access is package-private, not public. Confusing protected with 'only subclasses' — it also includes everything in the same package
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that default access (package-private) is deliberate API design, not a forgotten modifier. Show that protected is wider than most think — same package plus subclasses anywhere. Demonstrate real encapsulation through behavior-exposing methods, not field-exposing accessors

sections.title: Why Java Has Four Access Levels Instead of Just Public and Private
sections.content:
Most developers think in two levels: public or private. They mark fields `private`, add getters and setters, and call it encapsulation. But Java has **four** access levels for a reason, and the two in the middle — default (package-private) and protected — are where the real design decisions happen.

The core idea behind encapsulation isn't hiding data. It's **controlling the surface area of change.** When a class exposes a field or method, every piece of code that uses it becomes a dependency. Change the field type, rename the method, or alter its behavior, and all those dependents break. Access modifiers let you control exactly how wide that scope of change is.

`private` means only this class is affected by changes. `default` (package-private) means your package — your team's internal API — can use it, but nothing outside can depend on it. `protected` extends that to subclasses in other packages. `public` means anyone, anywhere, forever.

The reason most developers skip over default and protected is that IDEs autocomplete `private` and `public`, and the middle two rarely appear in basic examples. But in a codebase with well-structured packages, **the default access level is often the right choice** — it creates boundaries between modules without the ceremony of interfaces. Spring's internal classes use package-private extensively to hide implementation details from the public API while keeping them accessible to related classes in the same package.

sections.title: Four Access Levels at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|private|~This class only|fields, helpers, inner logic|no subclass, no package|default: hide everything
blue|package-private|~Same package only|no keyword — omit modifier|internal API design|Spring internals use this constantly
emerald|protected|~Package + subclasses|same package = yes too|subclasses in other pkgs|strictly wider than package-private
violet|public|~Everyone, everywhere|permanent API surface|removing it = breaking change|every public method = contract

sections.title: The Access Matrix: What Each Modifier Actually Allows
sections.content:
The four access levels form a strict hierarchy from narrowest to widest. The confusion usually lives in the middle two rows — protected is wider than most developers expect.

| Modifier | Same Class | Same Package | Subclass (other package) | Everywhere |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `private` | Yes | No | No | No |
| default (no modifier) | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| `protected` | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| `public` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |

The non-obvious detail: **`protected` includes same-package access.** A `protected` method is accessible to every class in the same package — not just subclasses. This means `protected` is strictly wider than default, not a different dimension. Many candidates say protected means "only subclasses," which is wrong.

Another trap: **there is no `default` keyword for access.** You simply omit the modifier. Writing `default` before a field is a syntax error. The term "package-private" is the community name for this level — Java's language spec calls it "default access."

When choosing a modifier, start narrow and widen only with reason. Can anyone outside this class ever need this? If no, `private`. If only classes in this package need it, omit the modifier.

If subclasses in other packages need it, `protected`. Only use `public` for your intentional API surface — once something is public, removing it is a breaking change.

sections.title: The Getter/Setter Trap: Private Fields With Accessors Is Not Encapsulation
sections.content:
Every Java tutorial teaches the same pattern: mark fields `private`, generate getters and setters. It looks right — the field is private, after all. But making a field `private` and adding `getBalance()` and `setBalance()` is not encapsulation. If external code can read and write the field through accessors, the field is effectively public — you've just added a layer of indirection that provides no actual protection.

Real encapsulation exposes behavior, not state. Instead of `account.setBalance(account.getBalance() - 100)`, the class offers `account.withdraw(100)`. The `withdraw` method validates the amount, checks for overdraft, logs the transaction, and updates the balance internally. The caller doesn't know or care how the balance is stored — it could be an `int`, a `BigDecimal`, or a database call.

This matters in practice because internal representation changes. A `BankAccount` class might start with `private int balance` and later move to `private BigDecimal balance` for precision. With real encapsulation, that change is invisible to callers — `withdraw()` still works. With getter/setter encapsulation, every caller that used `getBalance()` in arithmetic now has a type mismatch.

Lombok's `@Getter` and `@Setter` annotations make this worse by making it effortless to expose every field. Use `@Getter` sparingly — only on fields where external code genuinely needs to read the value — and avoid `@Setter` almost entirely. If a field needs to change, there should be a method that describes why it changes.

sections.title: Fake Encapsulation — Caller Drives All Logic
Real Encapsulation — Class Owns Its Invariants
Package-Private: The Modifier Senior Engineers Actually Reach For
sections.content:
Every tutorial teaches private and public. Package-private is the one almost never explained, which is exactly why it comes up in interviews about access modifiers.

You get package-private by omitting the modifier entirely — there is no `default` keyword. Writing `default int count` is a syntax error. Any class in the same package can access it; nothing outside the package can. This isn't a forgotten modifier or a lazy shortcut — it's deliberate module boundary design.

The use case: internal implementation classes. If you're building a payment processing package with five internal collaborators, but the only thing external code should ever see is `PaymentProcessor`, you make the four internal classes package-private. External code can't accidentally depend on them. Refactoring them doesn't break callers. Spring Framework does this constantly — if you browse the source of `spring-security`, you'll find dozens of package-private classes orchestrating the filter chain internally, invisible to your application code. Only the public contracts like `SecurityFilterChain` are part of the API.

The decision rule: start `private`, widen to package-private when other classes in the same package need access, widen to `protected` or `public` only when there's a concrete external need. Every public method or field is a contract you maintain forever.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **No modifier = package-private, not `public`** — there is no `default` keyword; you omit the modifier entirely.
- **`protected` includes the same package** — not just subclasses; "protected = only subclasses" is the most common wrong answer.
- **Getters/setters ≠ encapsulation** — `private balance + setBalance()` is effectively public; prefer `account.withdraw(100)`.
- **Start `private`, widen only with reason** — every `public` method is a permanent contract; removing it breaks callers.
- **Lombok `@Setter` on every field bypasses encapsulation** — prefer behavior methods that describe why state changes.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Encapsulation is about controlling the surface area of change — not just hiding fields. Every public method or field is a dependency: the wider you expose internals, the more places break when those internals change.

**What encapsulation actually means**
- Private fields plus getters/setters is indirection, not encapsulation — `account.setBalance(account.getBalance() - 100)` puts all the logic on the caller, with no validation, no overdraft check, no audit log
- Real encapsulation exposes behavior, not state: `account.withdraw(100)` keeps all of that inside the class
- Change `balance` from `double` to `BigDecimal` with real encapsulation — no callers notice, because they called `withdraw()`, never `getBalance()`

**The four access modifiers**
- `private` — class only; no modifier (package-private) — same package; `protected` — same package plus subclasses in other packages; `public` — everyone, permanently
- Interview trap: `protected` ≠ only subclasses — it includes the entire same package, making it strictly wider than package-private
- There is no `default` keyword — you omit the modifier. `default int count` is a syntax error.

**When to reach for each**
- Start `private` — widen only when there's a concrete reason
- Package-private (no modifier): internal classes the same package needs but nothing outside should touch
- Every `public` method is a permanent API contract — once external code depends on it, removing it is a breaking change

Lombok's `@Setter` on every field undoes this entirely. If a field needs to change, there should be a method that describes why — not a setter that just sets.

followup_questions: What is the difference between protected and package-private — which one allows same-package access?
Why doesn't making a field private and adding getters and setters constitute real encapsulation?
When would you choose package-private (no modifier) over private for a class or method?
How does Lombok's @Data or @Getter/@Setter annotation interact with encapsulation principles?
What makes a method suitable for the public API vs keeping it as an internal implementation detail?

questions.question: Inheritance in Java — IS-A Relationship, super Keyword, and Method Overriding
questions.title: Inheritance in Java — IS-A Relationship, super Keyword, and Method Overriding
questions.direct_answer: **Inheritance** = child acquires parent's properties/methods via `extends` — only valid when IS-A holds in every context (Liskov Substitution Principle). `super(args)` chains upward through ancestors; omit it and the compiler inserts `super()` automatically — missing no-arg constructor = compile error. Override rules: **same or wider access**, **covariant return** (child can return `Dog` where parent returns `Animal`), **narrower checked exceptions**. `static` methods are **hidden** (reference type decides), not overridden. Prefer composition over inheritance for code reuse.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands inheritance beyond syntax — can they explain the IS-A test, how super() chaining works, the rules of method overriding, and critically when inheritance is the wrong tool
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using inheritance for code reuse instead of genuine IS-A relationships. Not knowing that super() is called implicitly even when you don't write it. Forgetting that overriding requires same or wider access modifier
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Articulate the Liskov Substitution Principle in practical terms — a subclass must be usable anywhere the parent is expected without breaking behavior. Show awareness that composition is usually preferred over inheritance in modern Java

sections.title: Java Inheritance: IS-A Relationship, super Keyword, and Why It Can Break
sections.content:
Inheritance lets a child class acquire the fields and methods of a parent class using the `extends` keyword. `Dog extends Animal` — every Dog object automatically gets Animal's `name`, `age`, `eat()`, and `sleep()`, and can add its own `bark()` or override what it inherits. The child writes only what's different.

The IS-A relationship is the other half. A Dog **is** an Animal — which means a Dog can be used anywhere an Animal is expected. `Animal a = new Dog()` is valid. Call `a.eat()` and you get Dog's version if it overrides, Animal's version if it doesn't. This substitutability is what makes runtime polymorphism work — the JVM dispatches to the right implementation based on the actual object, not the variable type.

Java supports four inheritance types: **single** (Dog → Animal), **multilevel** (GoldenRetriever → Dog → Animal), **hierarchical** (Dog, Cat, Cow all extend Animal), and **multiple via interfaces** — not classes. Java bans multiple class inheritance because of the diamond problem: if two parents both define `speak()`, the compiler can't choose. Interfaces with `default` methods sidestep this.

The design question — when to use `extends` and when not to — is where most developers need more depth. The IS-A test has a catch: the relationship must hold in **every context**, not just today's. A Square mathematically is a Rectangle, but a `Rectangle` has independent `setWidth()` and `setHeight()`. A caller who sets width to 4 and height to 5 and expects area of 20 gets 25 from a Square. That's the **Liskov Substitution Principle**: if a child can't be substituted for its parent without breaking callers, the inheritance is wrong.

sections.title: Inheritance Concepts at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|IS-A Test|~Permanent identity check|Dog IS-A Animal ✓|Square IS-A Rectangle? ✗|if it fails → use composition
blue|super()|~Constructor chain|must be first line|compiler inserts if missing|chains up to Object(), then back down
emerald|Override Rules|~Same/wider access|covariant return OK|narrower exceptions only|@Override — always write it
violet|Static Hiding|~Not polymorphism|reference type decides|no vtable dispatch|method hiding, not overriding

sections.title: IS-A in Practice: Types of Inheritance and When the Test Fails
sections.content:
**IS-A** is a substitution test, not just a naming convention. If `Dog extends Animal`, then a Dog must work correctly anywhere an Animal is expected — same contract, same behavioral guarantees. The Dog/Animal case passes easily: Dog inherits `eat()` and `sleep()`, adding `bark()` doesn't break any existing Animal caller.

The four main inheritance types in Java all use relationships that genuinely pass this test:

- **Single**: `Dog extends Animal` — one child, one parent
- **Multilevel**: `Puppy extends Dog extends Animal` — a chain of specialization; each level IS-A its parent
- **Hierarchical**: `Dog`, `Cat`, `Cow` all extend `Animal` — multiple children, one common parent

**Multiple inheritance via classes is not allowed.** If `ClassC extends ClassA, ClassB` and both define `speak()`, the compiler has no rule to pick one — that's the diamond problem. Java solves this through interfaces: a class can implement many interfaces, and since Java 8, `default` methods can coexist because the implementing class can override them explicitly if there's a conflict.

**When IS-A fails — use composition.** Two services sharing validation logic are not in a parent-child relationship; they just have similar code. Making one extend the other ties them together permanently: change the parent's logic, and both children feel it. The alternative is composition — hold the shared behavior as a field (`HAS-A`) rather than inheriting it. You get the same reuse without the structural coupling.

The rule: if you can't honestly say 'B is genuinely a kind of A in every situation it will ever be used,' reach for composition instead.

sections.title: The super Keyword: Three Ways a Subclass Talks to Its Parent
Missing super() — The Compile Error That Appears on a Line You Didn't Write
Explicit super(args) — Chain to the Right Parent Constructor
Method Overriding Rules: What the Compiler Checks and What the JVM Does
sections.content:
Method overriding is how a child provides its own implementation of a method the parent defines. The `@Override` annotation tells the compiler to verify the override is valid. Without it, a typo in the method name silently creates a **new method** instead of overriding — no warning, and the parent's version runs at runtime.

**Same or wider access modifier.** A `protected` parent method can be overridden as `protected` or `public` in the child, never `private`. The reason connects to substitution: any caller that can call the method on the parent must be able to call it on the child. Narrowing access would break that guarantee.

**Covariant return type.** If the parent returns `Animal`, the child can return `Dog` — a more specific type. This was added in Java 5 and is used heavily in builder patterns: `Builder.setName()` can return `Builder`, while `AdvancedBuilder.setName()` returns `AdvancedBuilder` for fluent chaining without casting.

**Checked exceptions can only be narrower.** The child can throw fewer checked exceptions, or more specific subclasses of them, but never a broader exception. Callers catch what the parent's signature declares — if the child introduced something new, existing catch blocks wouldn't cover it.

**Static methods are hidden, not overridden.** If parent and child both define a static method with the same name, the version that runs depends on the **reference type** — not the object type. `Animal a = new Dog(); /* static call via a */` calls Animal's version. No vtable dispatch, no runtime resolution. This is the opposite of polymorphism, and it's a reliable interview trick question.

The practical rule: always write `@Override`. It costs nothing and catches bugs that are otherwise invisible at compile time.

sections.title: IS-A Violation: Why Square Inheriting Rectangle Breaks Callers
Key Points
sections.content:
- **IS-A must hold everywhere (Liskov)** — if swapping parent for child breaks any caller, the inheritance is wrong.
- **`super()` is inserted by the compiler** — omit it and the compiler adds the no-arg; no no-arg parent = compile error.
- **Override rules: same/wider access, covariant return, narrower checked exceptions** — static methods are hidden, not overridden.
- **Parent constructor + overridden method = null child fields** — vtable dispatches to child before child constructor runs.
- **Composition over inheritance** — when IS-A isn't permanent, prefer HAS-A; deep hierarchies are the most common Java design mistake.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Inheritance lets a child class acquire the fields and methods of a parent through `extends`. `Dog extends Animal` — Dog gets Animal's properties and can add or override them. The IS-A relationship is the foundation: a Dog is always an Animal, which means a Dog can stand in anywhere an Animal is expected. That substitutability is what makes runtime polymorphism possible — it's not just code sharing.

**IS-A and types**
- Three types: single (`Dog extends Animal`), multilevel (`GoldenRetriever extends Dog extends Animal`), hierarchical (`Dog`, `Cat`, `Cow` all extend `Animal`)
- Multiple via classes is not allowed — diamond problem. Use interfaces instead
- The IS-A test: must hold in every context, not just today's. A Square is mathematically a Rectangle, but a Rectangle caller expects independent width and height — Square breaks that. If the child can't honor the parent's contract, the inheritance is wrong

**The super keyword — three uses**
- `super.field` accesses a parent field shadowed by a same-name child field
- `super.method()` calls the parent's version of an overridden method — used when extending behavior, not replacing it
- `super(args)` calls the parent constructor; must be the first line. Omit it and the compiler inserts `super()` automatically — causes a compile error if the parent has no no-arg constructor

**Method overriding**
- Same or wider access: `protected` can become `public`, never `private`
- Covariant return: child can return a more specific type (`Dog` where parent returns `Animal`)
- Checked exceptions: only narrower — child can't introduce new ones the caller doesn't handle
- Static methods are hidden, not overridden — reference type decides which runs; always write `@Override`

The Liskov Substitution Principle is the interviewer checkpoint. It's the formal name for the IS-A test failing in context — Square-Rectangle is the example everyone expects. Knowing it by name and being able to explain why the code breaks is the answer that separates design-aware from syntax-level.

followup_questions: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle and how does the Square-Rectangle example violate it?
Why does Java insert super() automatically if you omit it — what happens if the parent has no no-arg constructor?
What is the difference between method hiding (static) and method overriding (instance)?
When should you always use @Override and what silent bug does omitting it cause?
What is the fragile base class problem and how does it motivate preferring composition?

questions.question: Compile-Time vs Runtime Polymorphism in Java
questions.title: Compile-Time vs Runtime Polymorphism in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Compile-time polymorphism** = method overloading — compiler picks the right method by parameter types at the call site (**reference type** decides). **Runtime polymorphism** = method overriding — JVM picks by actual object type at execution via vtable dispatch (**object type** decides). `Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak()` → calls `Dog`'s version. `static` methods are **hidden** not overridden — no vtable lookup, reference type wins.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can clearly distinguish method overloading (compile-time, resolved by parameter types) from method overriding (runtime, resolved by actual object type via vtable dispatch). Whether they understand dynamic method dispatch
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking overloading is polymorphism in the same sense as overriding. Not understanding that the compiler chooses the overloaded method based on the declared reference type, not the actual object type. Confusing method hiding (static) with overriding (instance)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the JVM mechanism — vtable dispatch for overriding vs simple signature matching at compile time for overloading. Mention that overloading resolution uses the reference type, which leads to surprising behavior with inheritance

sections.title: Polymorphism in Java: When the Compiler Decides vs When the JVM Decides
sections.content:
Ask a developer what polymorphism is and they'll say "same method, different behavior." Ask them to explain the difference between compile-time and runtime polymorphism, and you'll immediately see whether they understand the mechanism or just memorized a definition.

The distinction is about **when the decision is made.** Compile-time polymorphism — method overloading — means the compiler looks at the method signature you wrote (name + parameter types) and decides at compile time which method to call. This is a convenience feature: you can have `calculate(int)`, `calculate(double)`, and `calculate(int, int)` in the same class, and the compiler picks the right one based on what you pass.

Runtime polymorphism — method overriding — means the **JVM** decides at execution time. You have a variable typed as `Animal`, but the actual object is a `Dog`. When you call `animal.speak()`, the JVM looks at the real object type, finds `Dog`'s version of `speak()`, and calls that. The compiler can't know which version will run because the object could be created dynamically — from a factory, from a database, from user input.

This runtime decision is what makes polymorphism powerful. It's why you can write `List<Shape> shapes` and call `shape.draw()` on each one without knowing or caring whether it's a `Circle`, `Rectangle`, or `Triangle`. The code works with shapes that don't exist yet — shapes you'll add next month.

sections.title: Polymorphism Concepts at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Overloading|~Compile-time decision|same name, different params|reference type matters|syntactic convenience
blue|Overriding|~Runtime decision|JVM object type decides|vtable dispatch|architectural power
emerald|Dynamic Dispatch|~JVM vtable lookup|per class at runtime|Animal a = new Dog()|a.speak() → Dog's version
violet|Static Hiding|~NOT polymorphism|reference type decides|no vtable lookup|p.who() → Parent, not Child

sections.title: Compile-Time vs Runtime: When the Decision Happens and Why It Matters
sections.content:
The two forms of polymorphism differ in mechanism, timing, and purpose. The table makes the distinction concrete.

| Aspect | Compile-Time (Overloading) | Runtime (Overriding) |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Same method name, different parameter lists | Same method signature in parent and child |
| Decided by | Compiler, based on declared parameter types | JVM, based on actual object type at runtime |
| Which type matters | **Reference type** (declared type of variable) | **Object type** (actual instance created with `new`) |
| Keyword | None — just define multiple methods | `@Override` annotation (recommended) |
| Can cross classes | No — all overloads must be in the same class | Yes — parent method overridden in child class |
| Return type | Can differ freely | Must be same or covariant (more specific) |
| Access modifier | Can differ freely | Must be same or wider |

The row that trips people up: **which type matters.** With overloading, if you pass a `Dog` to a method that accepts `Animal`, the compiler resolves using the declared parameter type. With overriding, `Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak();` calls `Dog.speak()` because the JVM checks the actual object. This is **dynamic method dispatch** — the JVM uses a vtable (virtual method table) to look up the correct implementation at runtime.

The practical consequence: overloading is just syntactic convenience. Overriding is the mechanism that enables writing code against interfaces and abstract types — the foundation of pluggable architecture.

sections.title: Method Overloading: When the Compiler Makes the Call
Method Overriding: When the JVM Makes the Call at Runtime
sections.content:
Method overriding is resolved at runtime by the JVM, not the compiler. The compiler only verifies that the override is valid — same signature, compatible return type and exceptions. The actual dispatch happens when the method is called on a live object.

The mechanism is the **vtable** (virtual method table). Every class has one — a lookup table mapping method signatures to their concrete implementations. When you call `animal.speak()`, the JVM doesn't go to `Animal`'s `speak()`. It checks the actual object's class, looks up `speak()` in that class's vtable, and calls whatever implementation it finds there.

This is why runtime polymorphism is architecturally powerful. You can write code against the `Animal` interface without knowing which specific animal it is. When you add a new animal type next year, existing code works — no modifications, no recompilation of the callers.

One edge to know for interviews: **private methods can't be overridden.** They aren't in the vtable — they're resolved at compile time to the declaring class. If a parent's method calls a private helper and a child defines the same private method, the parent's method always calls the parent's version. The child's version is invisible to it.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Compile-time = overloading, runtime = overriding** — compiler resolves by parameter types; JVM resolves by actual object type.
- **Reference type picks overload; object type picks override** — `Animal a = new Dog()` picks the `Animal` overload, calls `Dog.speak()`.
- **Dynamic dispatch uses a vtable** — per-class virtual method table; method calls look up the real object's entry at runtime.
- **Static methods are hidden, not overridden** — reference type decides which runs, not the object type.
- **Overloading = convenience, overriding = architecture** — overriding is the mechanism behind every pluggable design in Java.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Polymorphism in Java means the same method call can produce different behavior depending on the object it's called on. Java achieves this two ways: overloading at compile time, and overriding at runtime. Most of what interviewers call "polymorphism" refers to the runtime kind — the mechanism that makes interface-based design actually work.

**Compile-time polymorphism — overloading:**
- Overloading lets you define multiple methods with the same name but different parameter types — the compiler resolves which version to call based on the declared argument types at the call site
- The key point is that the reference type decides, not the actual object: passing `Animal a = new Dog()` to an overloaded method runs the `Animal` version, because the compiler locked in its choice before the program ran
- Overloading is a naming convenience — it keeps your API clean by letting you write `draw(Circle)` and `draw(Rectangle)` instead of two different method names; it doesn't provide architectural flexibility

**Runtime polymorphism — overriding:**
- When you call an overridden method, the JVM uses a per-class virtual method table (vtable) to dispatch to the actual object's implementation — not the reference type's version
- `Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak()` calls `Dog.speak()` — the JVM checks Dog's vtable at execution time, even though the reference is declared as `Animal`
- This is what makes `List<Shape>` work: you iterate and call `shape.draw()` on each element, and the JVM routes to `Circle.draw()`, `Rectangle.draw()`, or whatever the real object is — no `instanceof` checks needed

**The static method trap:**
- Static methods are hidden, not overridden — they bypass the vtable entirely, so the declared reference type decides which version runs, not the actual object
- This is the standard interview trick: both parent and child define `static void display()` — calling it via an `Animal` reference always runs `Animal.display()` even when the object is a `Dog`; the object type is irrelevant

I recommend writing `@Override` on every intended override — without it, a mistyped method signature silently creates a new method or hides a static method instead of overriding, and the compiler gives no warning.

followup_questions: What is dynamic method dispatch and how does the JVM's vtable mechanism work?
If you pass a Dog reference typed as Animal to an overloaded method, which version runs — and why?
Can you override a static method in Java? What actually happens when you define the same static method in a subclass?
What is covariant return type in method overriding and when does it apply?
How does runtime polymorphism enable the open/closed principle in practice?

questions.question: Abstraction in Java — When to Use Abstract Class vs Interface
questions.title: Abstraction in Java — When to Use Abstract Class vs Interface
questions.direct_answer: **Abstract class** = identity (IS-A), can have instance state, constructors, `protected` methods — single inheritance only. **Interface** = capability (CAN-DO), multiple implementation, Java 8+ `default` methods. Decision rule: need shared instance fields or constructors? → abstract class. Defining a contract any class can fulfill? → interface (modern Java default). Adding a new `abstract` method breaks all subclasses; adding a `default` method to an interface is backward-compatible.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the design trade-off between abstract classes and interfaces — not just syntax differences, but when each is the right tool. Whether they know how Java 8 default methods blurred the line
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Listing syntax differences without explaining when to choose each. Not knowing that interfaces can have default methods since Java 8, which eliminated the main advantage of abstract classes for many use cases
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the real decision is about identity vs capability — abstract classes define what something IS, interfaces define what something CAN DO. Mention that a class can implement multiple interfaces but extend only one class, making interfaces the more flexible default

sections.title: The Decision Java 8 Made Harder: When 'Use an Interface' Stopped Being Obvious
sections.content:
Before Java 8, the choice was simple: need shared method implementations, use an abstract class; need a pure contract, use an interface.

Then Java 8 added **default methods** to interfaces, and the line blurred.

Now interfaces can have method bodies, static methods, and even private helper methods (Java 9+). So the question shifts from "do I need method implementations?" to something more fundamental: **am I defining what something IS, or what something CAN DO?**

An abstract class represents **identity** — a shared base that says "all subclasses are fundamentally this thing." `Animal` is an abstract class because `Dog` and `Cat` are animals at their core. They share state (name, age), behavior (eat, sleep), and a common identity.

An interface represents **capability** — a contract that says "this thing can do X." `Comparable`, `Serializable`, `Runnable` don't describe what something is. They describe something it can do.

A `Dog` might be `Comparable` and `Serializable`, but those aren't part of its identity.

The practical consequence of getting this wrong shows up when requirements change. If you made `Flyable` an abstract class, you can't have a `Duck` that's both an `Animal` and `Flyable` — Java has single inheritance. But if `Flyable` is an interface, a `Duck extends Animal implements Flyable` works perfectly. **Interfaces compose. Abstract classes don't.**

sections.title: Abstraction Concepts at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Interface|~100% abstraction|CAN-DO capability|multiple implements OK|Java 8+ default methods
blue|Abstract Class|~Partial abstraction|IS-A identity|shared state + behavior|single extends only
emerald|Default Methods|~Java 8 bridge|interface + implementation|backward-compatible evolution|forEach, stream on Collection
violet|Decision Rule|~Interface first|needs state or constructors? → abstract|pure contract? → interface|Spring = 100% interfaces

sections.title: Abstract Class vs Interface: The Complete Decision Matrix
sections.content:
The syntax differences matter less than the design implications. This table covers both.

| Aspect | Abstract Class | Interface |
|---|---|---|
| Inheritance | Single — `extends` one class only | Multiple — `implements` many interfaces |
| State (fields) | Instance fields, constructors | Constants only (`public static final`) |
| Method bodies | Always allowed | `default` methods (Java 8+), `private` (Java 9+) |
| Access modifiers | Any — `private`, `protected`, package | `public` only (methods are implicitly public) |
| Constructors | Yes — called via `super()` chain | No constructors |
| Design intent | IS-A identity — "this is fundamentally a..." | CAN-DO capability — "this can..." |
| Evolution | Adding abstract methods breaks all subclasses | Adding default methods is backward-compatible |

The evolution row is critical in large codebases. If you add a new abstract method to an abstract class, **every subclass must implement it immediately** — a breaking change across the codebase. Adding a `default` method to an interface is backward-compatible — existing implementations keep working. This is exactly why Java added default methods: to evolve `Collection` and `Iterable` without breaking every class that implemented them.

sections.title: The Decision Rule: Start With an Interface, Reach for Abstract Class Only When You Must
sections.content:
The interface is the default choice in modern Java. Reach for it whenever you're defining a contract or capability that multiple unrelated classes might implement — when callers should depend on an abstraction, not a specific type. The fact that a class can implement many interfaces but extend only one abstract class makes interfaces strictly more composable. `Duck implements Animal, Flyable, Serializable` is valid; inheriting all three is impossible.

Reach for an abstract class only when you need something interfaces still can't provide: shared instance state across subclasses, constructors or initialization logic, or non-public methods in the base type. The template method pattern is the classic use case — an abstract parent defines an algorithm skeleton and declares certain steps `abstract`, forcing subclasses to fill them in while sharing the orchestration logic and any state it depends on.

The evolution consideration is underrated in practice. If you add a new abstract method to an abstract class, every subclass must implement it immediately — a breaking change across the codebase. Adding a `default` method to an interface is backward-compatible; existing implementations keep working unchanged. This is exactly the route Java took when adding `forEach`, `stream`, and `removeIf` to `Collection` in Java 8 without breaking every existing implementation. If you find yourself writing an abstract class, ask whether the shared behavior could live in a `default` method or a composed helper instead — if it can, the interface gives you more flexibility with no trade-off.

sections.title: Coupled — Concrete Type Locks Every Caller to ArrayList
Abstracted — Callers Depend Only on the List Contract
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Identity vs capability** — abstract class = IS-A (what something is); interface = CAN-DO (what it can do).
- **Java 8+ default methods blurred the line** — interfaces can have method bodies; the decision now hinges on state and constructors.
- **Interfaces compose, abstract classes don't** — a class implements many interfaces but extends only one.
- **Adding abstract methods is a breaking change** — every subclass must implement immediately; adding `default` is backward-compatible.
- **Default to interfaces in modern Java** — use abstract classes only when you need shared instance state or non-public methods.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Abstraction in Java means hiding the implementation details and exposing only what the caller needs to work with. Java provides two mechanisms for this: interfaces, which define a pure contract with no implementation, and abstract classes, which allow a mix of abstract methods and concrete shared behavior. The distinction between them matters most when designing extensible systems.

**Interface — pure contract:**
- An interface defines what an object can do, not what it is — `Comparable`, `Serializable`, `Runnable` describe capabilities that any class can gain regardless of its inheritance hierarchy
- A class can implement many interfaces, which is how Java compensates for the lack of multiple inheritance — behavior composes horizontally through interfaces
- Since Java 8, interfaces can carry `default` method implementations — this was how `Collection.stream()` was added to millions of existing codebases without breaking anything

**Abstract class — shared implementation:**
- An abstract class makes sense when subclasses share mutable state (instance fields), initialization logic, or non-public helper methods that shouldn't be in an interface
- The template method pattern is the canonical use case: the abstract class defines the algorithm skeleton with abstract steps, and subclasses fill in the specific steps
- `Animal` as an abstract class works because `Dog` and `Cat` genuinely share `name`, `age`, and common behavior — it's an IS-A identity, not just a capability

**The Java 8 shift:**
- Before Java 8, "do I need a method implementation?" was the deciding question — that answer always pointed to abstract classes
- After Java 8, the real question is: do you need shared **state** (instance fields) or **constructors**? Only abstract classes can have those; interfaces can now have method bodies
- Adding a new `default` method to an interface is backward-compatible; adding a new `abstract` method to an abstract class immediately breaks every existing subclass

I recommend interfaces as the default in modern Java; reach for abstract classes only when you genuinely need shared mutable state or constructor logic that subclasses must run.
